title: Will Threejs just became a product like Unity, UE or Godot?
author: GeorgiaWitness1
selftext:
I have been a SWE for 10 years now. 

I remember Three.js was just a library to make charts. The same way Threejs now is used to make games, the same idea was used by Ryan Dahl to make Nodejs or Fordan walke used virtual DOM to create React. 

All use this basic concepts to create major pieces. 

Question: Is anyone already doing a GODOT with ThreeJS? You already can use WASM to generate performant engines, we see this everyday generated by Astra/Fable. Also Typrescript is already a performant enough to make the same job as C# does in unity, to call C++ to do the heavy lifting. 

Just ideas floating, and i don't see why not. Is not my cup of tea but i might do it for fun

comments.author: CycleMother2006
comments.body:
I highly doubt you can get anything near true C++ performance building on the bottleneck of JS. I would love to be proven wrong, as my main language for years has been JS and to a lesser extent Python. It was my biggest blocker building games before AI, since the games I wanted to built demanded significantly more power than JS libraries could really deliver.

I have had some fun with Pixi.js though, and have seen it chug through thousands of animated sprites on screen at once without any sign of hitching. So maybe there's something there for 2d, but you start seeing concerns when we're talking large scale physics or lighting simulations. Though the biggest issue I found was asset streaming. You really had to do a lot of targeted loading/unloading. It wasn't really forgiving if you allowed normal garbage functions to take place unless you were OK with sudden loading spikes (modded Minecraft can attest to this, too.)

All that said... I think Three.JS and Pixi.Js are extremely underrated. I think someone could definitely produce a hit game on them --- you could easily produce a better looking Runescape, for instance --- but the burden is really on the developer, and you give up a lot of free resources, plugins, etc that are time savers by attempting to do so. On the other hand, AI seems to do its best work in JS. So for a vibe coder it may not be a bad tradeoff.

replies.author: DaedalusRaistlin
replies.body:
It's actually in a pretty good spot. I have Vertex Animated Textures and gpu pathing for my swarm game. WebGPU let's you do stuff that wasnt easy before. 

I'm at over 100,000 3d models on screen, close to 60fps on a 3060 TI. Attacker and defender logic, destructable walls and compounds, siege engines, and lots of blood and bodies. 

It's not Ultimate Epic Battle Simulator 2 numbers of units in screen, but it's getting close to the first UEBS average numbers. I have a lot more optimising to do still.

replies.author: ledniv
replies.body:
I don't think JavaScript itself necessarily has to be the blocker here. You can apply Data-Oriented Design in JS using typed arrays and get much more predictable, cache-friendly data access.

For example, instead of 10,000 enemy objects:

    enemy.position.x
    enemy.position.y
    enemy.velocity

you can store the runtime data in contiguous arrays:

    const posX = new Float32Array(maxEnemies);
    const posY = new Float32Array(maxEnemies);
    const velocity = new Float32Array(maxEnemies);

Then process them in a tight loop. The CPU is reading sequential numeric data instead of jumping between thousands of JS objects, and you can preallocate everything so the GC stays out of the gameplay loop.

That's basically the same approach I use with Data-Oriented Design in Unity: arrays/data locality first, then add lower-level optimization tools only when profiling says you need them.
